subject: elephant
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module that constructs an elephant using the SDK's builder functions, drawing on the various joint, chain, sweep, loft, and surface operations available for shaping and detailing the model.

Since exact method signatures aren't fully known, I want to stay conservative and stick close to patterns shown in examples—using chains with path points for the spine, trunk, and tail, sweeps for tapered limbs, and parts for discrete geometry like tusks. For the overall anatomy, I'm thinking real-world elephant proportions: roughly 3 meters at the shoulder and about 5.5 meters long including the trunk, with a body formed by sweeping along a spine chain, four sturdy tapered legs, large flat ear shapes, spike-like tusks, and a tapering trunk and tail built from chains with varying sweep radius. I'm leaning toward grey for the body with maybe pinkish inner ears for contrast, and considering whether to layer in paint or decal calls for added surface detail.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton: placing a root pelvis joint near the back of the body around y=1.9, then building a spine chain running forward from the pelvis through the chest, with each point rising slightly and moving toward the front of the elephant to mimic a natural arch.

For body shape, rather than wrestling with sweep or loft functions with uncertain signatures, I'll fall back to scaling a sphere geometry and attaching it to the spine bone — scaling it wide on the sides and elongated front-to-back to get a convincing barrel-shaped torso, since basic mesh placement with scale options is much safer than guessing at more complex helper APIs.

For the trunk and limbs, I'm leaning toward building them as chains of rigid tapered cylinder segments attached to successive joints rather than trying to use smooth sweeps along curves. This keeps the look blocky and puppet-like, which fits the style, and sidesteps uncertainty about tapering/radius parameters in sweep functions. For legs, I'm setting up a joint hierarchy (hip, knee, ankle, foot) with parent relationships, and attaching thigh/shin frustum cylinders between each joint pair so the limb segments read as rigid rigged parts.

I'm defining explicit model-space coordinates for the spine and head joints (pelvis, chest, neck, head, jaw) rather than relying on a chain abstraction with roles, since I'm not certain how chain roles work—plain named joints with parent references should be safe and sufficient here.

Now I'm sizing the body sphere, computing scale factors to get the right height and depth from belly to back, then placing it on the pelvis bone. I'm doing the same for the head sphere, and sketching out the ears as extruded fan-shaped geometry flared outward with baked-in rotation, attached to the head bone.

For the ears, I'm rotating the shape so its flat plane faces sideways (roughly the YZ plane) instead of forward, positioning them on either side of the head. For the tusks, I'm using tapered cylinders rotated to point forward and slightly downward, figuring out which rotation maps the cylinder's axis correctly so the tip ends up pointing outward from the mouth.

I'm placing the tusk bases near the jaw joints and computing their world positions by offsetting from the base point along the rotated direction. Now I'm laying out the trunk as a chain of joints curving downward and forward from the head, tapering toward the tip.

For connecting segments between trunk joints, I'm avoiding the forbidden quaternion aiming method and instead checking whether the helper library's `part` function supports a `dir` option to orient cylinder geometry along an arbitrary direction, or whether there's a simpler `rod`/`capsule` helper that takes two endpoints directly.

Given the ambiguity, I'll settle on using a sweep function that takes a path of points and a radius to build the tapered trunk as several overlapping segments with progressively smaller radii, passing explicit bone references so each segment follows the right joint rather than relying on automatic nearest-bone detection.

For the legs, I'm planning four limbs with hip, knee, and ankle joints, building each thigh and lower leg as tapered sweeps between joint positions, then adding flattened sphere shapes for feet and pads positioned near the ankles. I'm placing front legs further forward and back legs further back along the z-axis, with legs spaced symmetrically on either side.

For the eyes, I'm positioning small black spheres on the front of the head, calculating their placement based on the head's scaled radius so they sit just on its surface.

For the tail, I'm sweeping a thin tapering path curving down and back from the pelvis, finishing with a small tuft sphere at the tip, and I'm settling on a color palette with grey tones for the body and darker shades for the legs, plus pink-ish inner ear plates layered over grey outer ears using offset extruded shapes. For the ears themselves, I'm using an elliptical shape extruded with a shallow depth and positioning them near the head's pivot point.

Now I'm working out the geometry positioning: rotating the ear shape so its thickness runs along the x-axis and its width wraps around toward the back of the head, then placing it on the side of the head with a slight outward tilt. I'm checking that the ear height doesn't awkwardly clip past the head's top, deciding to scale it down slightly so it tops out near the crown.

I'm defining the tusk attachment point near the mouth, then plotting the trunk's curve as a sequence of points flowing from the head down toward the ground, tapering in width as it goes.

I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy -- pelvis as root, neck and head as children, jaw and trunk attached to head, hips branching off the pelvis for the front and back legs -- and working out joint names that fit the naming rules along with approximate leg segment lengths down to the foot.

For the geometry, I'm settling on using cylinders for the thighs and lower legs since they're mostly vertical, each centered and tapered appropriately and bound to the hip/knee bones, plus a small cylinder pad at the ankle for the foot. The torso itself I'm building from a stretched sphere scaled unevenly and positioned on the pelvis bone to get the right body proportions.

I'm now sanity-checking proportions — making sure the legs sit inside the body's footprint, sizing the head sphere and verifying its top and front edges don't clip awkwardly against the body, and deciding the body-head junction doesn't need a separate neck piece since they already overlap enough. Then I'm placing small spheres for the eyes and checking their positions fall correctly on the ellipsoid head surface, before moving on to positioning the base and direction of the tusks.

Working through the tusk rotation math to get the curve and taper orientation right, then setting ivory coloring for them and considering where to anchor them on the jaw. I'm also sketching out the tail as a swept tube with a tuft at the end, and assigning the overall color palette for body, legs, ears, and the inner ear plates, figuring out the right offset and size for the inner ear shape relative to the outer ear.

Now I'm working through the ear thickness and mirroring math -- figuring out how the extrusion depth translates into x-position after the rotateY transforms for both the +X and -X ears, and confirming the mirrored ear keeps the same width orientation along z so the two sides stay symmetric.

I'm placing the pink inner plate 0.02 units further outward than the outer ear plate with a thinner extrusion depth, and treating the "at" coordinate as the geometry's center position for each ear part.

Now I'm sketching out the structure of the elephant body: using `b.part` for ear geometry attached to bones, `b.sweep` for the trunk and tail paths with color, and setting up the export metadata with name and description. I'm deciding to skip random wrinkle scatter for reliability and only importing the `createBuilder` function needed, then starting to write the actual module imports and builder setup.

Building out the skeleton joints...

Adding the head as a scaled sphere with a forehead dome for character, then working through trunk sweep segments with tapering radius for a tapered elephant trunk shape. Now I'm building the tusk geometry, rotating cylinders to angle outward from the head bone on each side.

Placing the eyes, ears, and tail with a sweep for the tail shape and a tuft sphere at the tip, checking that the tail base sits just outside the body silhouette and that joint positions line up correctly before verifying the lowest point for ground contact.
